newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Croatia again rapped for treatment of Serbs.
newsitem.headline: Croatia again rapped for treatment of Serbs.

text.p: The United Nations on Monday again chastised Croatia for failing to protect Serb residents on its territory and blocking the work of the international tribunal seeking suspected Croat war criminals.
A human rights report by Secretary-General Kofi Annan said Zagreb had made little progress in its treatment of minority Serbs since a similar report was submitted three months ago.

In particular, he said that statements from President Franjo Tudjman on the issue shed doubt "on the sincerity of the government's commitment" to allow Serbs to return home and treat those who stayed behind fairly. Croatia has said that Annan quoted Tudjman's Jan. 22 speech out of context.

The report also said Croatia, despite public statements to the contrary, had failed to arrest suspected war criminals indicted by the Hague-based tribunal on the former Yugoslavia. The government did not provide information, assistance and in general withheld cooperation.
The U.N. tribunal has indicted some 74 suspects -- 53 Serbs, 18 Croats and three Moslems. But most remain at large.
The Security Council reviews Croatia's human rights situation about every three months, a process the Zagreb government says singles it out unfairly.

Up to 200,000 Serbs fled when Zagreb's troops recaptured the Serb-dominated Krajina region in two swift offensives in mid-1995. Only a few Serbs remained in the area and about 14,000 have been allowed to return.

"Croatian Serbs continue to live in conditions of serious insecurity," the report said. "Incidents of looting and harassment remain common. Croatian police authorities are ineffective in restoring security"

Annan said that while most incidents are petty crimes, elderly Serbs feel isolated "and live in a constant state of fear." He said that a day after Elizabeth Rehn of Finland, the U.N. human rights investigator, visited the town of Knin, elderly Serbs were harrassed and their properties looted.
The report also said that little progress had been made in allowing young relatives of elderly Serbs who stayed behind during the 1995 offensives to return.

"There remains strong grounds for concern that the government is withholding its full cooperation," the report said adding that it had failed to provide "assistance and information" nor arrested suspects on its territory.
Croatia argues that the incidents against Serbs should be viewed as a natural crime rate rather than human rights violations and that all Croatians were paying the price of years of warfare.
